projects.t: Cardboard sheet-mulch bed with drip & plant-through holes
projects.why: Smother weeds and grass with wet, overlapping plain cardboard instead of plastic, run drip lines, and plant seedlings straight through holes you punch. The cardboard rots into the soil by the end of the season.
projects.deeper: Cardboard is a temporary barrier: it blocks light so weeds die back, holds moisture, and feeds soil life as it breaks down. Water has a harder time getting through dry cardboard, so put drip lines in place before you plant through it and check the soil underneath with your finger.
steps: Pick a sunny spot. Mow or cut weeds and grass as short as you can; leave the roots — the cardboard will smother them.
Peel off every bit of tape, labels and staples. Use only plain brown cardboard.
Soak the cardboard in a tub of water (or hose it until soft) so it bends and lies flat against the ground.
Lay it down in strips that overlap 6–8 in, like shingles, so no light or weeds can sneak through the seams.
Run 2–3 drip lines along the bed and pin them with landscape staples. Run the water for a minute to check every line drips.
Cover the cardboard with a few inches of compost or wood-chip mulch to hold it down and keep it from drying out.
Where each plant goes, punch or cut an X through the cardboard with a dibber or knife, pull the flaps back and plant the seedling in the soil below.
Water the seedlings in well. For hot sun, add a shade-cloth low tunnel over the bed (see "Low tunnel with shade cloth").
when: Best: lay it 2 months before planting
Or set it up in fall for next spring
projects.season: Fall (to plant next spring) or early spring — plant through it right away if you add compost on top.
pros: No digging and no plastic to throw away
Smothers lawn and weeds while it feeds the soil
cons: Tough perennial weeds (bindweed, quackgrass) can push through — overlap well
Dry cardboard sheds water: drip lines help
Slugs like to hide under it in wet weather
safety: Skip glossy, waxy, printed or colored cardboard and pull off all tape and labels — colorful inks can contain heavy metals and tape is plastic.
Call 811 before you drive stakes or dig if you are near buried utility lines.

mats.item: Plain brown corrugated cardboard (no tape, labels, glossy or colored print)
mats.qty: enough to cover the bed with 6–8 in overlaps
2–3 lines the length of the bed

mats.item: Large tub or kiddie pool for soaking

projects.why: Build a new bed on top of lawn by stacking cardboard and alternating layers of “greens” and “browns”. Let it rest a few months and it turns into rich, loose soil.
projects.deeper: It is a slow compost pile spread flat. The browns (leaves, straw, shredded paper) bring carbon; the greens (grass clippings, kitchen scraps, manure that is already composted) bring nitrogen. Fall-built beds are ready by spring.
steps: Mow the area short and outline the bed (3–4 ft wide is easy to reach across).
Lay wet cardboard with wide overlaps.
Add a 2–3 in brown layer, then a 1–2 in green layer. Water each layer until it is damp like a wrung-out sponge.
Keep stacking until the pile is 12–18 in tall — it will sink a lot.
Finish with 2–3 in of compost.
Let it rest about 2 months (fall to spring is ideal), then plant into the top layer.
when: or late winter for late-spring planting
projects.season: Fall is best — leaves are free and it has all winter to break down.
cons: Takes months before it is ready
Shrinks as it rots — top it up each year
safety: Do not add meat, dairy, pet waste or fresh manure to beds you will eat from.
Same cardboard rule: plain brown only, tape removed.

mats.item: Green layers: grass clippings, vegetable scraps, coffee grounds

projects.why: Stop turning the soil. Smother the weeds, add a thick layer of compost on top each year and plant into it — the soil keeps its crumbly structure and fewer weed seeds come up.
projects.deeper: Tilling breaks apart the soil crumbs (aggregates) that hold air and water. In a no-dig bed earthworms and roots do the mixing. Keep paths separate so you never step where you grow.
steps: Mark out beds narrow enough to reach the middle without stepping in (about 4 ft).
Cut weeds at ground level; leave roots in place.
Cover with cardboard and wet it thoroughly.
Spread about 6 in of good compost on top.
Plant seeds or transplants straight into the compost.
Each year, add a fresh inch or two of compost and pull weeds while small instead of digging.
pros: Better soil structure year after year
cons: Compost for a big area costs money
safety: Buy compost from a supplier who can tell you what is in it; avoid compost made with treated wood.

mats.item: Plain brown cardboard or thick newspaper
Mulch for paths (wood chips or straw)

more.t: No-Dig Garden Beds (UF/IFAS Extension Solutions for Your Life)

projects.why: Pile logs and branches, cover them with sod, compost and soil, and grow on the mound. The wood soaks up water like a sponge as it rots.
projects.deeper: It is an old European practice that is popular with permaculture gardeners. Be realistic: extension specialists point out there are no peer-reviewed studies proving the claims, and rotting wood can tie up nitrogen for a while — so feed the first crops.
steps: Pick a spot and dig a shallow trench (optional) the length of the bed.
Lay the largest logs first, then branches, then small twigs to fill gaps.
Soak the wood well.
Add upside-down sod, leaves and clippings to fill the spaces.
Cap with 4–6 in of compost and soil, then mulch the sides so they do not wash off.
Plant squash, potatoes or other hungry crops the first year and feed them with nitrogen.
cons: Nitrogen can be short at first; the mound sinks
safety: Never bury pressure-treated, painted or railroad-tie wood.
Lift with your legs, wear gloves and eye protection when cutting branches.

mats.item: Logs and branches (untreated, not black walnut, cedar or other slow/allelopathic woods)
Sod turned upside down, leaves, grass clippings

projects.why: A 4 × 8 ft box 10–12 in deep warms up early in spring, drains well and is easy on the back. Fill it with a mix of topsoil and compost.
projects.deeper: Untreated lumber starts rotting within a year or two but is safe; naturally rot-resistant cedar or redwood lasts much longer. Modern ACQ / copper-based treated lumber is allowed around food by many extension services, but if you are unsure, use cedar or line the inside with plastic. Never use old CCA (arsenic) wood or railroad ties.
steps: Choose a level spot with 6–8 hours of sun. Keep it 4 ft wide or less so you can reach the middle.
Cut boards to length (most stores cut for free).
Screw each corner to a 4×4 post, pre-drilling to avoid splitting.
Set the frame in place, level it, and remove sod or cover the ground with cardboard.
Staple hardware cloth to the bottom if burrowing animals are a problem.
Fill with a topsoil + compost blend, rake level and water to settle it.
projects.season: Any time the ground is not frozen.
pros: Fewer weeds; no stepping on soil
safety: Never use CCA-treated wood (older, arsenic), railroad ties or creosote.
Wear eye protection when cutting; keep power tools away from kids.

mats.item: Hardware cloth for the bottom (gophers/voles, optional)

projects.t: Raised bed — concrete block or metal
projects.why: Stack concrete blocks (no mortar needed for one or two courses) or bolt together a corrugated-metal kit. Both last for decades.
projects.deeper: Blocks can raise the soil pH a little over time — a soil test every few years tells you. Metal beds heat up in full sun; a light-colored finish and mulch help. You can plant herbs or strawberries in the block holes.
steps: Level the ground along the outline — block beds wobble on slopes.
Lay the first course of blocks tight together; check level often.
For metal kits, bolt the panels together following the kit instructions and brace long sides.
Cover the bottom with cardboard, then fill with soil and compost.
Plant herbs or strawberries in the block cavities if you like.
pros: Block holes give extra planting pockets
safety: Concrete blocks are heavy — lift with your legs and wear gloves.
Metal edges can be sharp; cover the top edge with trim.

mats.qty: about 20 for a 4×8 bed one course high

mats.item: or a galvanized/powder-coated metal bed kit

more.t: Raised Beds - Materials List (corrugated steel beds, in-ground and free-standing, 4' x 8') - WSU Extension

projects.why: No yard? Grow tomatoes, peppers, herbs and greens in buckets and pots on a balcony, patio or driveway.
projects.deeper: Bigger pots dry out slower. A container that is wider than tall is steadier in wind. Gravel in the bottom does NOT improve drainage — holes do. Use potting mix, not garden soil.
steps: Drill 4–6 holes (½ in) in the bottom of each bucket, plus a few low on the sides.
Set each bucket on bricks or a saucer so water can drain.
Fill with damp potting mix to 1 in below the rim; mix in fertilizer.
Plant one tomato or pepper per bucket (or several greens/herbs).
Water until it drains out the bottom; check daily in summer.
projects.season: Spring after frost (cool crops a little earlier).
pros: Move plants to the sun or out of a storm
cons: Big pots are heavy when wet
safety: Use food-grade buckets (HDPE #2) that never held chemicals, paint or solvents.

mats.item: Saucers or bricks to lift the pots

more.t: Vegetable Gardening in Small Spaces (NC State Extension)

projects.why: Nest one bucket inside another: the bottom holds a water reservoir and a wicking cup pulls water up into the potting mix. Water every few days instead of every day.
projects.deeper: The plant drinks from below, so leaves stay dry and moisture stays even — great for tomatoes that crack or get blossom-end rot when watering swings. Add a small overflow hole so rain does not drown the roots.
steps: Cut the top bucket’s bottom with many small holes and one hole for the wicking cup in the center, plus one for the fill tube near the edge.
Drill an overflow hole in the outer bucket just below where the inner bucket’s bottom sits.
Nest the buckets; push the wicking cup through the center hole and the fill pipe through its hole.
Pack damp potting mix firmly into the wicking cup first, then fill the bucket.
Plant, water from the top once, then fill the reservoir through the pipe until water runs out of the overflow.
pros: Water every 2–4 days instead of daily
cons: Reservoir can breed mosquitoes if left open
Salts build up — flush with plain water now and then
safety: Use food-grade buckets only.
Cover the fill tube so mosquitoes cannot breed.

mats.item: Plastic cup or net pot (wicking cup)

projects.why: Plant right into “conditioned” straw bales — a raised bed with no frame and no soil. Great on poor soil or even a driveway.
projects.deeper: For about 10 days you water the bales and feed them nitrogen so they start composting inside. They heat up; wait until the inside has cooled to about body temperature before you plant.
steps: Set bales cut-side up, strings on the sides, in full sun. They will be too heavy to move once wet.
Water each bale until it is soaked.
For about 10 days, sprinkle nitrogen on top and water it in on a schedule (heavy feeding days alternate with water-only days).
Push a thermometer in: plant only once the inside is 99 °F or cooler.
Pull open planting pockets, add a handful of potting mix and set transplants in.
Water often — bales drain fast.
projects.season: Spring, about two weeks before your planting date.
pros: Bales become compost after one season
cons: Needs lots of water and fertilizer
Straw may have weed or grain seeds
Bales break down by season end
safety: Ask the seller whether the straw was sprayed with persistent herbicides (aminopyralid / clopyralid) — they can harm tomatoes and beans.
Wear gloves when handling fertilizer and wash your hands.

mats.item: Straw bales (wheat or oat straw — not hay)
Nitrogen fertilizer (urea, ammonium sulfate or blood meal)
mats.qty: about 3 lb per bale over 10 days
a few handfuls per planting hole

projects.t: Keyhole bed with a compost basket
projects.why: A round, raised bed with a compost basket in the middle and a notch to walk in. Kitchen scraps and water go in the center and feed the whole bed.
projects.deeper: Developed for dry climates: the center basket keeps nutrients and moisture flowing outward, and the bed slopes down from the middle so water spreads. Typical size is 6–8 ft across and 2–3 ft high.
steps: Mark a 6–8 ft circle with a string and stake. Mark a pie-slice notch on the north side (south side in the Southern Hemisphere) so you can reach the center.
Build the center basket from wire mesh and stand it up.
Build the outer wall about 2–3 ft high, leaving the notch open.
Fill the bottom with cardboard, branches and leaves, then topsoil and compost, sloping down from the basket to the wall.
Fill the basket with greens and browns; add scraps and water there all season.
cons: Lots of stone and soil to move
safety: Keep walls stable and no taller than kids can safely reach over.
Keep meat and dairy out of the basket.

mats.item: Stones, blocks or bricks for the wall
mats.qty: enough for a 6–8 ft circle, 2–3 ft high

mats.item: Wire mesh or sticks for the compost basket

projects.why: Put water right at the roots with drip tubing and emitters on a simple timer. Less water, drier leaves, fewer diseases.
projects.deeper: A basic kit is: faucet → backflow preventer → pressure regulator → filter → ½ in mainline → drip lines or emitters along each row. A 100-mesh filter keeps emitters from clogging. Run it in the morning, longer and less often, so water soaks deep.
steps: Sketch your beds and measure the run from the faucet.
Attach backflow preventer, pressure regulator and filter at the faucet (that order).
Lay the ½ in mainline along the head of the beds; cap the far end.
Punch holes and connect drip lines down each bed — about 12 in apart for most vegetables.
Pin lines with staples, flush the system with the end caps open, then close them.
Run it and dig down a few inches to check that water reaches the roots; set the timer.
projects.season: Spring at planting; drain and store before hard freezes.
pros: Works with a timer while you are away
cons: Emitters can clog or get chewed
safety: Always use a backflow preventer so garden water cannot flow back into drinking water.

mats.item: ¼ in drip line or inline emitter tubing
Barbed connectors, tees, end caps, goof plugs

photo.title: Drip irrigation lines with a filter in a mulched vegetable garden

more.t: Installing Drip Irrigation in Home Gardens (Clemson HGIC 1268, 2026)
Using Drip Irrigation in the Garden (Iowa State University Extension Yard and Garden, reviewed Feb 2026)

projects.why: The easiest drip system: a porous hose that sweats water along its whole length. Snake it through the bed, cover with mulch and turn it on.
projects.deeper: Soaker hoses work best on short, level runs (under about 100 ft) with low pressure. Use a pressure-reducing washer or open the faucet only a little.
steps: Lay the soaker hose along your plants, a few inches from the stems.
Pin it down at bends with staples.
Connect to a regular hose with a pressure reducer.
Cover with mulch to slow evaporation.
Run it 30–60 minutes, then dig down to see how deep the water went; adjust.
cons: Uneven on slopes or long runs
Wears out in a few seasons
Hard to tell how much water went out
safety: Don’t leave a soaker hose pressurized in hot sun with the end capped for days — it can burst.

projects.why: Catch roof water in a covered barrel to water flowers, lawns and young trees. Use it carefully on food crops.
projects.deeper: Roof water picks up bird droppings, shingle grit and anything else on the roof, so it is NOT drinkable. Extension services advise against using it on vegetables you eat; if you do, water the soil (never the leaves), do it early in the morning, and wash produce well. Screens keep mosquitoes out.
steps: Pick a downspout and level a base of blocks — a full barrel weighs over 400 lb.
Drill and fit the spigot near the bottom and the overflow near the top.
Screen the inlet so mosquitoes and leaves stay out.
Cut the downspout and fit the diverter, or route it into the screened top.
Point the overflow away from your foundation.
Label the spigot “Do not drink” and empty or disconnect it before freezing weather.
projects.season: Spring; drain it before hard freezes.
cons: Not safe to drink; limited use on edibles
safety: Rain-barrel water is not drinkable. Label the spigot “Do not drink”.
Use it on soil, not leaves or produce; water early in the day and wash produce well. Many extension services say not to use it on edibles at all.
Keep a tight screen so mosquitoes cannot breed; keep lids child-safe.

mats.item: Food-grade 55-gallon drum or a rain-barrel kit
Fine mesh screen for the top

projects.why: Bury an unglazed clay pot up to its neck next to your plants and keep it filled. Water seeps slowly through the clay right to the roots.
projects.deeper: Ollas are an ancient method used in dry regions. You can make one by gluing two unglazed terracotta pots rim-to-rim and plugging the bottom hole. Plants within about a foot of the pot benefit most.
steps: For DIY: seal the bottom hole of one pot and glue the two pots rim to rim; let it cure fully.
Dig a hole and bury the olla up to its neck in the middle of a group of plants.
Plant seedlings around it, within about a foot.
Fill it with water and cover the top.
Check every few days and top up — it empties faster in heat.
projects.season: At planting; lift before hard freezes so it does not crack.
safety: Keep it covered so kids, pets and mosquitoes stay out.

mats.item: Unglazed clay olla, or 2 matching unglazed terracotta pots
Waterproof, non-toxic silicone or epoxy (for DIY pots)
A lid, tile or saucer for the top

projects.why: A 2–3 in layer of mulch keeps soil moist, cool and weed-free. Pick the right kind for each spot.
projects.deeper: Straw and shredded leaves are great on vegetable beds. Wood chips are best for paths and around shrubs. Grass clippings work in thin layers. Plastic and landscape fabric warm the soil but do not feed it. Keep mulch an inch or two away from stems.
steps: Weed and water the bed first.
Wait until the soil warms in spring before mulching warm-season crops.
Spread 2–3 in of mulch, leaving a ring of bare soil around each stem.
Use thicker wood chips on paths.
Top up as it breaks down.
projects.season: Late spring after the soil warms; again in fall.
safety: Avoid grass clippings from lawns treated with weed killers.
Ask suppliers about persistent herbicides in straw, hay and manure.

mats.item: Straw (seed-free), shredded leaves or grass clippings for beds

projects.t: Low tunnel with shade cloth (rebar + flexible hoops)
projects.why: Drive rebar stakes along the bed, slide flexible tubing over them as hoops, tie a ridge rope along the top and pull a cover over: shade cloth for summer heat, row cover for frost, insect netting for pests.
projects.deeper: Low tunnels 15–30 in high with hoops 2–4 ft apart are easy to build. Shade cloth (30–50%) cools lettuce and greens in hot weather and slows bolting. In spring and fall swap to row cover, which protects down to about 24–28 °F; clear 6-mil poly gives more warmth but must be vented on sunny days.
steps: Mark both sides of the bed with stakes every 2–4 ft (closer in windy or snowy places).
Drive rebar about 12 in into the ground at each mark, leaving 12 in above, angled very slightly outward.
Slide one end of a tube over a rebar, bend it over the bed and slide the other end over the matching rebar. Aim for 15–30 in tall.
Tie a rope along the top of every hoop from end to end and anchor it to a stake at each end so the hoops stay upright and evenly spaced.
Pull the cover over, clip it to the hoops and weigh down the edges and ends with sandbags or soil.
Cap or flag all exposed rebar so nobody trips or gets hurt.
Open one side on hot, sunny days if you use plastic or heavy row cover; take shade cloth off when the heat wave breaks.
pros: Cheap and quick to put up or take down
One frame works for shade, frost and insects
Extends spring and fall by weeks
cons: Wind can rip covers if not anchored
Low height — only for short crops
safety: Cap or flag rebar — exposed ends cause injuries.
Call 811 before driving stakes near buried lines.
Uncover crops that need bees to pollinate when they flower (squash, cucumbers).

mats.item: Flexible tubing (½–¾ in PEX, poly or PVC) for hoops
Rope or strapping for the ridge line
Shade cloth 30–50% (summer) or floating row cover (spring/fall)
Clips, clothespins or sandbags to hold the cover

projects.why: Lay a light fabric right over plants (or over hoops) on cold nights. It traps soil heat and keeps light frost off the leaves.
projects.deeper: Floating row covers come in weights. Light covers let most light through and work as insect barriers; heavier frost cloth gives several degrees more protection but blocks more light. Plastic touching leaves can freeze them — use fabric, or hold plastic up on hoops.
steps: Check the forecast — cover before sunset when frost is predicted.
Drape the fabric loosely so plants can push it up as they grow.
Weigh down every edge so wind cannot get under it.
Remove or open it during warm days, and when crops that need bees start flowering.
Dry and fold it for reuse.
pros: Light enough to lie on plants
cons: Only a few degrees of protection
Hides pests that are already inside
safety: Anchor well so it cannot blow into roads or power lines.

photo.title: Floating row cover over a vegetable crop

more.t: Row Covers (Utah State University Extension, Dec 2020)

projects.why: A bottomless box with a clear, slanted lid. It catches the sun so you can harden off seedlings in spring and grow lettuce and spinach well into winter.
projects.deeper: Face the low side toward the sun (south in the Northern Hemisphere). The biggest risk is overheating, not cold: prop the lid open on sunny days above about 45 °F. An old window works if it has no lead paint.
steps: Pick a spot with full winter sun, sheltered from wind, low side facing south.
Cut the sides at a slant from the tall back to the short front.
Screw the box together at the corners.
Hinge the lid to the back so it lifts up; add a prop stick.
Set the box on loosened soil or over a bed, and fill gaps at the base.
Vent it on sunny days and close it before evening.
projects.season: Late winter through spring, and fall into winter.
cons: Cooks plants if you forget to vent
safety: Old windows may have lead paint — test or use polycarbonate.
Hinge lids so they cannot slam on fingers; add a stop.

mats.item: Boards for the box (cedar or untreated)
mats.qty: back 18 in tall, front 12 in, 3×6 ft

mats.item: Clear lid: polycarbonate, an old window (lead-free) or 6-mil plastic on a frame
Prop stick or automatic vent opener

projects.why: A walk-in tunnel of steel or PVC bows slipped over ground stakes and covered in greenhouse plastic. Grow tomatoes earlier and greens later.
projects.deeper: “Caterpillar” tunnels use bows on rebar or tubular stakes, held with ropes between bows instead of a heavy frame, so they can be moved. Roll up the sides for ventilation; take the plastic off or tighten it before big winds and snow.
steps: Lay out a level rectangle and mark stake spots every 5–6 ft on both sides.
Drive stakes, leaving equal heights above ground.
Slide bows over the stakes and tie a ridge rope or purlin along the top.
Pull the plastic over on a calm day, gather and tie the ends to stakes.
Run ropes over the plastic between bows down to anchors so wind cannot lift it.
Roll up the sides on warm days for ventilation.
projects.season: Late winter or early fall (calm day for the plastic).
safety: Take plastic off or reinforce before high winds and heavy snow.
Cap stakes and wear eye protection when driving them.

mats.item: Bows: galvanized steel hoops, electrical conduit or PVC
Ground stakes: rebar or tubular steel

projects.why: Cut the bottom off a clear milk or water jug and set it over a seedling — an instant mini greenhouse for cold nights.
projects.deeper: Push the cut edge into the soil so it does not blow away. Take the cap off on sunny days so the plant does not overheat; put it back on frosty nights.
steps: Rinse the jug and cut off the bottom.
Set it over the seedling and push the edge an inch into the soil.
Leave the cap off on warm days, put it on for cold nights.
Remove once nights stay above about 50 °F or the plant touches the sides.
cons: Blows over if not pushed in
safety: Cut away from your hands — adults handle the knife.

projects.why: Cover crops with fine mesh to keep out cabbage worms, flea beetles, squash vine borers and other pests — no spraying.
projects.deeper: Netting only works if pests are not already in the soil or on the plants, so cover right after planting and seal the edges. Uncover squash, cucumbers and melons when female flowers open so bees can pollinate.
steps: Rotate crops so overwintering pests are not inside the tunnel.
Plant, then install hoops right away.
Cover and seal every edge with soil or sandbags.
Check weekly under the netting for pests.
Open vine crops at flowering for pollination.
safety: Keep netting tight and weighted so birds do not get tangled.

mats.item: Insect netting or lightweight row cover
Sandbags or soil to seal edges

projects.why: Keep rabbits out with low chicken wire or hardware cloth buried a few inches deep; keep deer out with a tall fence.
projects.deeper: Rabbits: a fence about 2 ft tall with the bottom buried a few inches stops most of them. Deer: they jump, so plan on 6–8 ft or an electric or double fence design.
steps: Measure the perimeter and mark a gate spot.
Drive posts every 8–10 ft; brace the corners.
For rabbits, dig a shallow trench and bury the bottom of the wire 3–6 in, bent outward.
For deer, hang tall mesh from the posts and tie it every foot.
Install the gate and walk the fence each week for gaps.
projects.season: Before the season or after harvest.
safety: Call 811 before driving posts.
Follow the label and local rules for electric fence chargers; add warning signs.

mats.item: Chicken wire or ¼–1 in hardware cloth (rabbits)

projects.why: Bend a 16-ft livestock panel into an arch between two beds and grow beans, cucumbers or small squash over it — a shady walk-through tunnel.
projects.deeper: Panels are heavy welded wire. Two people bend them; T-posts or wooden frames inside the bed ends hold the feet. Fruit hangs down inside the arch where it is easy to see and pick.
steps: Place two beds 4–6 ft apart (the arch spans the path).
Drive two T-posts inside the inside edge of each bed.
With a helper, bow the panel and set each end against the posts inside the beds.
Tie the panel to the posts in several places.
Plant climbing crops at the base on both sides and guide vines up.
safety: Cut wire ends are sharp — wear gloves and eye protection; file or cover cut ends.
The panel springs back hard when bent; hold it with a helper.

projects.why: Two lean-to panels hinged at the top form an A. Cucumbers, peas and beans climb both sides and you can grow lettuce in the shade underneath.
projects.deeper: Use wood frames covered with wire mesh or netting. A spacer at the top keeps the sides apart; the A shape stands on its own and folds flat for storage.
steps: Build two rectangular frames 4 ft wide and 6 ft tall.
Staple wire or netting across each frame.
Hinge the frames together along the top edge.
Stand it over the row and push the feet into the soil or stake them.
Plant on both sides and guide vines up.
safety: Stake it down in windy spots; never let kids climb it.

mats.item: Welded wire fencing or trellis netting

projects.why: Hang a sturdy top bar or wire over the row and drop a string to each plant. Wind the plant around the string as it grows — cheap and space-saving.
projects.deeper: Works well for indeterminate tomatoes pruned to one or two stems, and for cucumbers. Use a strong overhead support (posts plus a pipe or wire) because a fruit-laden row is heavy.
steps: Drive a post at each end of the row and fix the top bar across.
Tie a string to the top bar above each plant.
Tie the bottom loosely around the stem base or to a stake (never tight).
Every few days, wind the growing tip around the string clockwise.
Prune tomato suckers if growing on one or two stems.
safety: Make sure the top bar is secured; a full row can weigh hundreds of pounds.

mats.item: Top bar: EMT conduit or heavy wire

photo.title: Runner beans climbing a vertical frame

projects.why: Strong cages or stakes keep tomatoes off the ground — cleaner fruit, less rot and disease.
projects.deeper: Store-bought cone cages are too small for big tomatoes. Make tall cages from concrete reinforcing wire (6-in openings for your hand). Staked plants give larger, earlier fruit; caged plants need less work but fruit is a bit smaller and later.
steps: Cut a 5 ft length of wire and bend it into a cylinder about 18–20 in across.
Hook the cut ends together.
Set cages or drive stakes at planting so you do not tear roots later.
Anchor each cage with two stakes.
Tie staked plants loosely every foot as they grow.
safety: Wear gloves and eye protection cutting wire; bend or file sharp ends.

projects.why: Stand a pallet or wall planter upright and grow herbs, lettuce and strawberries in pockets — great on fences and balconies.
projects.deeper: Only use pallets stamped HT (heat-treated). Pallets stamped MB were fumigated with methyl bromide and should never be used for food. Line the pockets with landscape fabric and water often — vertical planters dry out fast.
steps: Check the stamp — use only HT pallets with no stains or spills.
Sand rough spots and pull out loose nails.
Staple landscape fabric behind and under each slat row to make pockets.
Lay the pallet flat, fill with potting mix and plant.
Leave it flat 1–2 weeks so roots hold the soil, then stand it up and secure it to a wall or post.
safety: Never use pallets marked MB (methyl bromide) or of unknown origin for food crops.
Anchor upright pallets so they cannot tip onto kids.

mats.item: Pallet stamped HT (heat-treated) or a wall planter
Screws or brackets to secure it

projects.why: Three side-by-side bins: one to fill, one to cook, one finished. Turn from bin to bin and you get a steady supply of compost.
projects.deeper: Mix about 2–3 parts browns (dry leaves, straw) to 1 part greens (grass, kitchen scraps) by volume and keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Turning weekly can give finished compost in a couple of months; no starter is needed.
steps: Pick a level, shady spot near the garden and a hose.
Build three 3-ft cubes side by side sharing walls; leave the fronts open with slots for removable slats.
Fill bin 1 with layers of browns and greens, watering as you go.
When bin 1 is full, fork it into bin 2 and start filling bin 1 again.
Move bin 2 into bin 3 to finish. Use it when it is dark, crumbly and smells earthy.
projects.season: Any time; fall gives the most leaves.
safety: No meat, dairy, oils or pet waste.
Wear gloves and wash hands after handling compost.

projects.why: A closed drum on a stand that you spin to mix. Tidy, critter-resistant and good for small yards.
projects.deeper: Tumblers hold less than bins and can get too wet; add browns (shredded paper, leaves) with every bucket of scraps. Stop adding new material once it is two-thirds full so it can finish.
steps: Assemble it on level ground near the kitchen door.
Add greens and browns in roughly equal buckets.
Spin it a few turns every few days.
Squeeze a handful: it should feel damp, not dripping. Add browns if wet, water if dry.
When full, let it finish while you fill a second batch or bin.
safety: Lift heavy drums with care; keep fingers away from the spinning frame.

mats.item: Compost tumbler (kit or DIY barrel on a frame)

projects.why: Red wiggler worms turn kitchen scraps into rich castings in a bin under the sink, in the garage or on a balcony.
projects.deeper: Use red wigglers (Eisenia fetida), not earthworms from the garden. A good rule: about 1 cubic foot of bin space per pound of scraps a week. Keep the bedding as damp as a wrung-out sponge and between about 55 and 77 °F.
steps: Drill air holes in the lid and upper sides, plus small drain holes in the bottom.
Prepare the bedding: soak shredded paper, wring it out and fluff it into the bin with a handful of soil.
Add the worms and let them settle a few days.
Bury small amounts of fruit and vegetable scraps under the bedding, rotating spots.
In 3–6 months, move the finished castings to one side, add fresh bedding to the other and harvest when the worms move over.
projects.season: Any time — it can live indoors.
cons: Worms die if too hot, cold or wet
Fruit flies if scraps are exposed
safety: No meat, dairy, oily food or pet waste.
Wash hands after handling.

mats.qty: enough to fill ¾ of the bin

projects.why: Pile fall leaves, wet them and wait. In a year or two they turn into dark, crumbly leaf mold — a fantastic mulch and soil conditioner.
projects.deeper: Leaf mold is made mostly by fungi, so it is slow but easy. Shredding the leaves first (run the mower over them) speeds it up. A ring of wire fencing keeps the pile tidy.
steps: Rake leaves and shred them with the mower if you can.
Pile them in a wire ring or stuff them into bags with a few holes.
Wet them thoroughly and pack them down.
Leave them — check moisture now and then.
In 1–2 years use the crumbly leaf mold as mulch or mix it into beds and potting mix.
cons: Low in nutrients (it is a soil conditioner)
safety: Skip leaves from black walnut and leaves gathered from roadsides (possible contamination).

mats.qty: as many as you can get

mats.item: Wire fencing ring 3–4 ft across, or large bags

projects.why: Sow cereal rye, oats, crimson clover or hairy vetch in empty beds after harvest. They hold the soil over winter and add organic matter (legumes add nitrogen) when turned in or cut in spring.
projects.deeper: Most cover crops go in late summer or early fall, after warm-season crops. Cut or mow them before they set seed, and wait a couple of weeks before planting so they break down.
steps: Clear spent crops and weeds.
Loosen the top inch of soil with a rake.
Scatter seed evenly, rake it in lightly and water.
Let it grow over fall and winter.
In spring, cut it down before it flowers or sets seed; leave as mulch or turn it in and wait 2–3 weeks before planting.
cons: Rye can be tough to cut
Can reseed if left too long
safety: Hairy vetch and rye can be hard to kill if allowed to set seed — cut on time.

mats.item: Cover crop seed (cereal rye, oats, crimson clover, hairy vetch)
mats.qty: about ¼–½ lb per 100 sq ft

projects.t: How to take a soil test
projects.why: Find out your pH and nutrients before you add fertilizer or lime. Your state’s extension lab will tell you exactly what to add.
projects.deeper: Take 10–15 small samples from around the bed, all at the same depth (about 6 in for vegetables), mix them in a clean bucket and send a cup to the lab. Test every 3–4 years, in the same season each time.
steps: Get a kit or form from your county extension office.
For each area, take 10–15 small samples in a zigzag, all at the same depth (about 6 in).
Remove roots, stones and mulch; mix them in a clean bucket.
Let the mix air-dry, fill the bag to the line and label it.
Mail it; log the results here under Soil tests and follow the lab’s recommendations.
when: Fall is best (time to add lime)
projects.season: Fall or early spring, same season each time.
cons: Home kits are less accurate than labs
safety: Ask for a lead test for older urban yards and areas near old painted buildings.

mats.item: Soil sample bag or zip bag + lab form

projects.why: You do not need a shed full of gear. Start with a few good tools that match your garden type and add as you grow. Track what you own and what is on your wishlist in the Tools inventory.
projects.deeper: Buy fewer, better tools: forged steel heads, solid handles, and a size that fits your hands. A spade with a sharp edge cuts sod and heavy soil; a trowel plants; a hoe weeds; pruners harvest and trim.
steps: Open the Tools inventory and pick your garden type.
Mark what you already own.
Add missing essentials to your wishlist or shopping list.
Buy the best quality you can afford for tools you use every week.
Keep them clean, sharp and stored out of the rain (see “Tool care & sharpening”).
projects.season: Late winter (sales!) before the season starts.
pros: Avoid buying gadgets you never use
cons: Good tools cost more up front
safety: Store sharp tools hung up, blades away from walkways and kids.

projects.why: Clean, sharp, oiled tools work faster, last decades and spread fewer plant diseases.
projects.deeper: Clean soil off after each use. Disinfect pruners between diseased plants with 70% rubbing alcohol. Sharpen hoes and spades with a flat mill file at their original angle; rub boiled linseed oil into wooden handles each fall.
steps: Knock off soil and scrub with a wire brush; dry completely.
Remove rust with steel wool or sandpaper.
Clamp the tool and file the edge at its original angle, pushing away from you; finish pruners on a stone.
Wipe metal with a light coat of oil.
Lightly sand wooden handles and rub in boiled linseed oil.
Store indoors, hung up.
projects.season: End of season, and touch-ups during the year.
safety: Wear gloves and eye protection when filing.
Rags soaked with linseed oil can catch fire on their own — lay them flat to dry outside or soak them in water before throwing out.
Alcohol is flammable; never mix bleach with other cleaners.
